reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A chronic condition marked by progressive atrophy of the nasal mucosa and underlying turbinate bone, producing an abnormally wide nasal cavity
Classic features are foul-smelling greenish crusts (ozaena), a characteristic odour the patient often cannot perceive, and a paradoxical sensation of nasal blockage despite a roomy nose
Loss of smell (anosmia) and recurrent epistaxis when crusts are removed are common complaints

Primary disease affects young adults, more often women, and is more prevalent in some warmer regions, while secondary disease follows extensive nasal surgery, granulomatous disease, irradiation, or chronic infection
Examination shows a wide cavity with the nasopharynx visible beyond the abundant crusting, and turbinates appear shrunken
Management centres on nasal hygiene with regular saline or alkaline douching and removal of crusts, together with measures to keep the mucosa moist
Medical measures aim to reduce crusting and odour, and surgical narrowing of the nasal cavity is reserved for resistant cases
Secondary atrophic rhinitis warrants a search for an underlying cause such as granulomatous or specific infective disease
reference.pathophysiology: In atrophic rhinitis the respiratory epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia and the seromucinous glands, cilia, and nerve endings are lost, while the turbinate bone resorbs. The nasal cavity therefore widens abnormally and loses its normal humidifying and self-cleaning function, so secretions dry into thick crusts that are colonised by organisms (classically Klebsiella ozaenae) producing the foetid odour. Proposed contributors include chronic infection, nutritional deficiency, endocrine and hereditary factors, and autonomic imbalance; secondary forms follow destruction of mucosa by surgery, radiotherapy, trauma, or granulomatous disease.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) affecting the nose
Empty nose syndrome after turbinate surgery
additionalInvestigations: Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to document mucosal atrophy, crusting, and a widened cavity
Culture of nasal secretions where secondary bacterial colonisation is suspected
Biopsy and specific tests to exclude granulomatous or infective causes in secondary disease
Computed tomography to assess turbinate and sinus changes in atypical or secondary cases
Screening for nutritional deficiency where clinically relevant
redFlags: Crusting with cartilage or septal destruction, saddling, or systemic features suggesting granulomatosis with polyangiitis or another granulomatous disease
Unilateral crusting or a mass suggesting neoplasia rather than atrophic rhinitis
Persistent bleeding or crusting that fails to respond and needs biopsy
Signs of intracranial or orbital spread of an underlying destructive process
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and tends to persist for years; symptoms can be well controlled with diligent nasal hygiene and moisturising measures, and surgical narrowing helps selected refractory cases, but complete cure of primary disease is uncommon and secondary disease depends on treating its cause.
pitfalls: Labelling all nasal crusting as primary atrophic rhinitis without excluding granulomatous or malignant disease
Overlooking the paradox of a blocked feeling in a wide nasal cavity and offering decongestants that worsen dryness
Aggressive turbinate surgery that can itself precipitate secondary atrophic change
Failing to investigate secondary causes when disease is unilateral or atypical
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Centre management on nasal hygiene with regular saline or alkaline nasal douching and mechanical removal of the adherent crusts
Keep the mucosa moist with emollient nasal drops or ointments such as glucose-glycerine preparations or oils to reduce crusting and odour
Treat secondary bacterial colonisation, classically with Klebsiella, using topical or systemic antibiotics guided by culture
Treat the underlying cause in secondary disease and correct any relevant nutritional deficiency
Offer surgical narrowing of the nasal cavity, such as medialisation of the lateral wall or submucosal implants, for refractory cases
Provide ongoing ENT follow-up and educate the patient on the need for long-term maintenance of nasal hygiene
